reference.source: Hand surgery and sports medicine references
clinicalPearls: Avulsion of the flexor digitorum profundus tendon from its insertion on the distal phalanx, causing loss of active flexion of the fingertip
It classically occurs when a gripping finger is forcibly extended, as in grabbing an opponent's jersey
The ring finger is the most commonly affected digit
The patient cannot actively flex the distal interphalangeal joint of the involved finger when it is isolated
The retracted tendon end may be palpable more proximally, and the level of retraction guides urgency of repair
It is a surgical injury, and early diagnosis improves the outcome, as greater retraction compromises repair
reference.pathophysiology: Jersey finger results from sudden forced extension of a finger during active flexion, generating tension that avulses the flexor digitorum profundus tendon from the distal phalanx, sometimes with a bony fragment. Once detached, the tendon retracts proximally to a degree determined by whether its vincular blood supply and the fibro-osseous pulleys remain attached; greater retraction jeopardises the tendon's nutrition and complicates repair. Loss of the profundus insertion abolishes active flexion at the distal interphalangeal joint.
additionalInvestigations: Clinical testing of isolated distal interphalangeal joint flexion
Radiographs to detect a bony avulsion fragment and its position
Ultrasound or MRI to locate the retracted tendon end
Assessment of the level of tendon retraction
redFlags: Marked proximal retraction of the tendon threatening viability
reference.prognosis: Early surgical repair or reattachment generally restores good function, but delayed diagnosis, significant retraction or chronic injury can necessitate more complex reconstruction with poorer outcomes.
pitfalls: Missing the injury by not testing isolated distal interphalangeal flexion
Delaying referral so that the tendon retracts further
management: Prompt surgical reattachment or repair of the avulsed flexor digitorum profundus tendon, the definitive treatment
Early referral to hand surgery, as greater tendon retraction compromises repair and dictates urgency
Protective splinting and immobilisation of the finger while awaiting surgery to limit further retraction
Tendon reconstruction or grafting, or distal interphalangeal joint arthrodesis, for chronic or irreparable injuries
Radiographic assessment for a bony avulsion fragment to guide the repair technique
Structured post-operative hand therapy with a graded tendon-protection and mobilisation protocol
